newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: HK urges Australia investors to put faith in China.
newsitem.headline: HK urges Australia investors to put faith in China.

text.p: Hong Kong business leaders and top civil servants on Thursday wound up a tour of Australia where they tried to soothe concerns about Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule and urged investors to put some faith in Beijing.

The Hong Kong delegation, led by Chief Secretary Anson Chan, admitted there would be "bumps along the road" after China resumed control of the British colony next July, but played down unease expressed about the territory's economic future.
"Reports of our death are premature," Chan quipped to hundreds of Australian businessmen in Melbourne, where the delegation held the second of two business forums in Australia.
"There will of course be bumps along the road, but we will overcome them as we have in the past," she said.

Earlier, in a reflection of some anxiety encountered in the week-long roadshow, a businessman drew audience applause when he quizzed the delegation on fears about Hong Kong's continued freedom of information and legal independence.
Australia is a major investor in Hong Kong, with about 350 Australian firms operating in the territory.

Warning against undue alarm, a panel of businessmen and civil servants said Hong Kong's handover was likely to be a "non-event", but one senior trade official admitted the world awaited the first real test of the territory's new status.

Hong Kong Trade Development Council chief Michael Sze said the selection this year of an inaugural Hong Kong chief executive as the territory's new political leader would be an early test of China's commitment to Hong Kong's autonomy.
"The greatest test that we have is towards the end of this year to see what chief executive will emerge -- whether it's someone who will stick up for...our system," Sze said.
Under the principles laid down for the handover, Beijing has agreed to rule Hong Kong as an autonomous self-governing region under the notion of "one country, two systems".

Hong Kong business leaders, including Hang Seng Bank Ltd chief executive Alexander Au and Cathay Pacific airline managing director Rod Eddington, also sought to ease concerns about the transition to Chinese rule.
Australian-born Eddington told the forum that Hong Kong would remain the main gateway for foreign investment in China.

"As China becomes an increasingly important force in international trade...so this role can only grow," said Eddington, tipped by airline sources to return home ahead of the handover to become chief of loss-making Ansett Australia.
Eddington declined to comment on the speculation.
Hang Seng Bank's Au, asked about the knock-on effects of any banking crisis in China, assured businessmen Beijing would come to the rescue of its state banks in the event of such a crisis.
But, he added: "We don't detect any situation that would lead us to concern."
